message.content: In domestic cats and many other felids, the presence of a mane (the long, shaggy fur that develops around the head and neck of adult males) is controlled by a dominant allele. In lions, the same principle applies: the allele that codes for a mane is dominant over the allele that codes for a “mane‑less” phenotype. As a result, most male lions inherit the mane allele from at least one parent and develop the characteristic mane during puberty, while females (who typically do not carry the dominant allele in the same way) remain mane‑less. This dominant trait is one of the key genetic differences that distinguishes male lions from females and contributes to their social and reproductive roles within prides.
